articleBlocks: Paper and Storm make sand feel possible fairly quickly, but Wood can make the board seem messier than a clean shared-word puzzle. The opening clues stay ambiguous until Castle gives the board a cleaner test, so this guide starts with the misleading first read, then uses the later clues to show why the final connection is narrower than the early guesses and how each clue checks that same pattern without relying on the answer reveal too early.
Dollar helps because sand dollar proves the same beginning works in a beach phrase instead of only in weather or tools.

Once sandcastle appears, sandpaper, sandstorm, sand dollar, and even the slightly trickier sandalwood all make sense as the same sand-led family.

solutionNarrative: Paper made sand feel possible right away, and Storm reinforced it, but Wood kept the board from feeling solved because sandalwood is not as neat on the page as the other members. Dollar helped by showing the same beginning in a very different context.
Castle finished the job. Once sandcastle came to mind, the board stopped feeling inconsistent and started reading as a sand-led phrase family with one deliberately awkward member in sandalwood.

lessons.title: One awkward clue does not break a real pattern
lessons.body: A phrase board can still be valid when one member looks less clean than the others; often that clue is there to stop the solve from being too quick.

lessons.title: Lock with the most visual phrase you know
lessons.body: Sandcastle works because it is such a vivid, fixed image that it can stabilize the whole board once sand becomes plausible.

lessons.title: Compound boards often cross domains
lessons.body: Tools, weather, beach life, and fragrance words can all live under the same beginning, which is why staying flexible matters.
